title: Celibacy and married priests (CCC 1579–1580)
hook: Latin priests are usually celibate; Eastern Catholic churches ordain married men

segments.voice: Yesterday, three degrees: bishop, priest and deacon, one sacrament held three ways. Your line was three orders. Did you learn a name? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred six.

'Father, is that your wife?' A first-time visitor asks it at coffee hour, after the Divine Liturgy at an Eastern Catholic parish, and then wishes she hadn't. But the priest just laughs and says yes, and those are his three kids by the donut table. She had always assumed a Catholic priest couldn't be married. Across town, the Roman-rite pastor would tell her that he promised celibacy at his ordination, and means to keep it. Both men are Catholic priests. Both are in full communion with the pope. Today's word explains how that can be true.
screen: `FATHER, IS THAT YOUR WIFE?` → `YES, AND THREE KIDS.` → `ACROSS TOWN, A CELIBATE PASTOR.`

segments.voice: The Catechism tells it as two disciplines, side by side. In the Latin Church, it says, ordained ministers, except permanent deacons, are normally chosen from among men of faith who live a celibate life and intend to stay celibate. Celibacy means not marrying, for the sake of the kingdom of God. The Catechism calls it a sign of a new life, given over to the Lord and to his people, and points to a saying of Jesus in Matthew about those who give up marriage for the kingdom of heaven. The priest, in that picture, gives himself with an undivided heart to the Lord and to his people. Then the Catechism turns east. In the Eastern Churches, it says, a different discipline has long been in force. Bishops are chosen only from among celibates. But married men can be ordained deacons and priests. The Catechism calls this practice legitimate, and says these married priests bear real fruit in their communities. It adds that celibacy is held in great honor in the East as well, and that many priests there choose it freely. And in the East as in the West, it says, a man who has already been ordained can no longer marry. The order matters: marriage first, then ordination. Notice that the Gospels themselves hold both pictures. Jesus speaks of giving up marriage for the kingdom. And Peter, the apostle Jesus called the rock, had a mother-in-law: the Gospels tell of Jesus healing her of a fever in Peter's house. The Catechism presents two disciplines, not two priesthoods. The Church holds two traditions inside one communion, and honors both. Let's look back at the week. The fruits of Communion. Conversion, a lifelong turn. Many forms of penance. Indulgences, honestly. What anointing does. The three degrees of Holy Orders. And today, celibacy and married priests: one Church, two traditions.
screen: `THE LATIN CHURCH: NORMALLY CELIBATE.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF THE KINGDOM.` · `THE EAST: MARRIED MEN ORDAINED.` · `PETER HAD A MOTHER-IN-LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for priests' families. Settle, and breathe. A priest has a family too: parents who raised him, brothers and sisters, and for some, a wife and children who share his time with a whole parish. Picture one of those families. A mother who waits for a phone call. A child whose father is called out at dinner to a hospital. If you pray, you can ask God to bless them. If you don't, just hold them kindly in mind. The bell holds the time.

Celibacy. Not marrying, for the sake of the kingdom of God: the usual discipline for Latin priests, and the rule for bishops in the East, where married men may be ordained deacons and priests. Today's word.
Your line: two traditions. Today, when someone says all Catholic priests are unmarried, you'll know the fuller picture. Day one thousand one hundred six.

howItsDone: In the Latin Church, candidates for the priesthood normally promise celibacy when they are ordained; in Eastern Catholic churches, married men may be ordained deacons and priests, while bishops are chosen from among celibate clergy.

myth: in the Eastern Churches married men can be ordained deacons and priests, the Catechism says.

fork.setup: a married man in an Eastern Catholic church feels called to the priesthood. what does the Catechism allow?
options: he must leave his marriage first.
married men can be ordained deacons and priests.
he can only become a bishop.
fork.reveal: in the Eastern Churches married men can be ordained deacons and priests. bishops are chosen from among celibates.

trapdoor: what you thought: Catholic priests can never be married.
what it means: the Latin Church normally ordains celibate men; the Eastern Churches ordain married men as deacons and priests.
what a scholar hears: a discipline, not a doctrine of the priesthood's nature; two traditions held side by side in one communion.
recall: the faithful not ordained or vowed

notes: CCC 1579–1580 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). 'A different discipline has long been in force' follows CCC 1580's 'for many centuries', softened under the claims rule.
'Many priests there choose it freely' paraphrases CCC 1580's note that many priests in the East have freely chosen celibacy; confirm, or cut 'many'.
'Marriage first, then ordination' is the general Eastern practice; not stated in CCC 1580. Confirm.
'Celibacy is a discipline and a gift, not a rule written into the nature of the priesthood': a common way to put it; confirm phrasing for this path.
'The apostle Jesus called the rock' refers to Matthew 16:18.

Hook rewritten so it does not echo day 1093 (two churches a few streets apart). The scene is invented; 'three kids' is a scene detail, not a claim. Married Eastern Catholic priests outside their home territories have been restricted by local rules in some places; kept general.

Editor: 'marriage first, then ordination' now rests on CCC 1580's statement that an ordained man can no longer marry; cut the uncited claim that celibacy is 'not a rule written into the nature of the priesthood' (now 'two disciplines, not two priesthoods'); 'free to belong to everyone' replaced with the undivided-heart paraphrase; practice's 'every priest' softened.
Audit (2026-10-02): checked against CCC 1579–1580 and Mark 1:29–31; fixed a doubled 'The Catechism adds' in the teach. Content otherwise accurate.
